newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian banks' real estate exposure raises concerns.
newsitem.headline: Asian banks' real estate exposure raises concerns.

text.p: Asian banks' heavy exposure to real estate has raised concerns about their health should growth in regional property prices fizzle out, but these fears may be overdone, analysts in Singapore said on Tuesday.
Jitters over the real estate markets have beset the region since a crisis in Thailand early this year brought on by a credit squeeze and excess supply.
More recently worries have surfaced in the Philippines, where a number of property developers are believed to have over-extended themselves, depressing the Manila stock market.

"As Asia developed -- and the construction sector has been at the forefront of this growth -- we have had a concentration of bank lending towards the property market," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian Currencies Research at BZW.
Stephen Frost, associate research director at UBS Securities, estimated total bank lending for real estate, construction and mortgages in Asia, excluding Korea and Japan, was close to $200 billion.
"Loans to real estate account for 20 to 40 percent of total bank loans in most Asian markets," he said.

A slowdown in key export industries and the prospects of higher U.S. interest rates -- which can influence Asian rates through the dollar's link with regional currencies -- meant many Asian markets faced slow growth compounded by tighter credit.

On March 28, Malaysia's central bank moved to limit property lending by commercial banks to 20 percent of overall outstanding loans in what many analysts saw as a pre-emptive strike against further problems.
"These are absolutely the correct moves. The difficulty is, are they going to be able to implement those measures," said Wong Yit Fan, chief economist, Southeast Asia, for Standard Chartered Bank.

Analysts say Asian central banks have been proactive on this issue. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the so-called "central bankers' bank", has set capital adequacy ratios for commercial banks at eight percent.
But in Asia, capital adequacy requirements set by local central banks range from 16 percent in the Philippines to 11 percent in Thailand and 13 percent in Hong Kong.
Analysts also pointed out that the region continued to maintain high rates of growth which would generate the incomes needed to afford the properties being built.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) said last week that economic growth in the region was expected to remain at a strong 7.4 percent for 1997 and 1998. Growth was 7.4 percent in 1996, down from 8.2 percent the previous year, the ADB said.
"The key question is whether economic growth will be sustained to allow incomes to rise and allow affordability to catch up," said Standard Chartered's Wong.
The two factors of economic growth and adequately provisioned banks should limit the risk of any systemic crisis in the financial system from a slowdown in property prices.

"The conditions are there for the property market to slow regionwide," said BZW's Supple. "If it is in tandem with the slowdown in the rest of the economy there should be no serious systemic risk to the financial sector," Supple said,
However, Frost at UBS urged investors to be more circumspect.

"The party is coming to an end...once anecdotal stories of specific developers being in trouble emerge in any of these markets, don't wait for further confirmations of the downside risk. It is already there."
